questions.q: Bana, a scholar patronised by Harsha, wrote a literary work that is regarded as one of the world's first novels. What is it called?
questions.a: Kadambari, Bana's 7th-century novel; his Harshacharita is a biography of Harsha, not the novel.

questions.q: The chapter compares Xuanzang with Faxian, the Chinese pilgrim met in Part 1 of the textbook. Which statement is true of both of them?
o: Both came to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers
Both visited India during the reign of Harshavardhana
Both came in the 5th century and wrote about the Gupta court
Both were silk traders who carried Buddhist texts to sell in China
questions.a: Both came to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn doctrines from Indian teachers; Faxian came in the 5th century (Gupta era) and Xuanzang about two centuries later, between 630 and 644.

questions.q: (a) In which year, and at which city, did Harshavardhana ascend the throne? (b) Name the dynasty he belonged to.
questions.a: (a) In 606 CE at Kannauj. (b) The Pushyabhuti (or Vardhana) dynasty, whose earlier capital was Sthaneshvara (present-day Thanesar in Haryana).
s: States 606 CE and Kannauj
Names the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty

questions.q: True or False: Harsha succeeded in extending his empire southward beyond the Narmada. Give the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Harsha attempted to extend his empire southward beyond the Narmada but was held in check by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: he was held in check beyond the Narmada by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II

questions.q: Harsha dreamed of uniting northern India. (a) Name the dynasty he formed an alliance with, and the region it ruled. (b) What object found at Nalanda is linked to this ally? (c) Explain why this alliance still did not make Harsha the master of all northern India.
questions.a: (a) The Varman dynasty of Kamarupa, in today's Assam (capital Pragjyotisha, close to today's Guwahati). (b) A terracotta seal issued by King Bhaskaravarman of the Varman dynasty, Harsha's ally. (c) Conflicts with neighbouring kingdoms continued, so his dream of uniting northern India met with only mixed success; one ally in the east did not end the other rivalries, and in the south he was held in check by Pulakeshin II.
s: Names the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa (Assam)
Identifies the terracotta seal of King Bhaskaravarman found at Nalanda
Explains that conflicts with neighbouring kingdoms continued, so success was only mixed

questions.q:
Students of a Lucknow school are staging a play about a Chinese pilgrim's journey. The script notes say: the pilgrim travelled around the subcontinent for 14 years, ending in 644, and went home with more than 600 manuscripts of Buddhist texts in Sanskrit, carried by 20 horses. The director wants a final scene showing what he did with the manuscripts back in China, and a narrator's closing line on why his record matters to us today.
(a) Name the pilgrim and the year in which his travels in India began.
(b) If the manuscripts were shared equally among the horses, on average more than how many did each horse carry?
(c) What did the pilgrim do with the manuscripts once he was back in China?
(d) The draft closing line says, 'His record matters only to Buddhists.' Do you agree? Rewrite the line and justify it from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Xuanzang; 644 - 14 = 630, so his travels began in 630. (b) 600 / 20 = 30, so each horse carried more than 30 manuscripts on average (the chapter says 'more than 600'). (c) He set about translating them into Chinese. (d) No. He left a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion in the kingdoms he crossed (for example his picture of Kannauj and of Harsha as a just and energetic ruler), and his travelogue is a major source for historians of the period. A better line: 'His record is one of our main windows on India in the 7th century, not only on its Buddhism.'
s: (a) Xuanzang, travels began in 630
(b) 600 / 20 = 30, so more than 30 per horse on average
(c) Translated the texts into Chinese
(d) Disagrees: his account covers politics, diplomacy, culture and religion and is a major source for historians; gives a rewritten line

questions.q: Prepare a profile card on Harshavardhana for your class wall. Write one line for each heading: (a) the earlier capital of his dynasty and its present-day name; (b) the god inscriptions show him devoted to, and the other religion other sources link him to; (c) what he did at Prayaga every five years; (d) how Xuanzang described the city of Kannauj; (e) what the Banskhera copper plate signature says.
questions.a: (a) Sthaneshvara, present-day Thanesar in Haryana. (b) Inscriptions show him as a devotee of Shiva; other sources say he was also deeply attached to Buddhism, while respecting all schools of thought. (c) He held an assembly at Prayaga (present-day Prayagraj) where, after sacred rites, he gave away much wealth to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor. (d) As a beautiful and prosperous city. (e) 'By my own hand, the great king of kings, Shri Harsha'.
s: (a) Sthaneshvara, now Thanesar in Haryana
(b) Shiva in inscriptions; also attached to Buddhism
(c) Assembly at Prayaga where he gave away wealth to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor
(d) Kannauj described as beautiful and prosperous
(e) 'By my own hand, the great king of kings, Shri Harsha'

questions.q: Which of these was NOT one of the three powers in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj?
questions.a: The Chalukyas; the three warring parties were the Palas from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan.

questions.q: Each college of Vikramashila had a dvarapandita. Which present-day practice is closest to his role?
o: A scholar setting and judging an entrance test before a student is admitted
A guard checking that every visitor carries an identity card at the gate
A clerk collecting the fee before a student may enter the classroom
A librarian lending books to students at the door of the library
questions.a: A scholar setting and judging an entrance test: the dvarapandita ('scholar gatekeeper') tested students before allowing them entry, which made admission highly selective.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Gopala  2. Dharmapala  3. Somapura  4. Bakhtiyar Khilji
Column II: P. Founded major monasteries such as Vikramashila  Q. Chosen by the people in 750 CE to restore stability in Bengal  R. Plundered and destroyed Vikramashila in the 12th century  S. A major monastery in present-day Bangladesh
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Gopala was chosen by the people in 750 CE; Dharmapala founded monasteries such as Vikramashila; Somapura is a monastery in present-day Bangladesh; Bakhtiyar Khilji plundered Vikramashila in the 12th century.

questions.q: The chapter says large monasteries such as Vikramashila were 'in effect, the universities of those times'. Give two features of Vikramashila that support this description.
questions.a: Any two: it had six colleges, lecture halls and a vast library; nearly 3,000 scholars studied subjects such as grammar, logic, and Hindu and Buddhist philosophy; admission was selective, with a scholar gatekeeper testing students; it attracted students from far away, even beyond India.
s: First feature, e.g. six colleges, lecture halls and a vast library
Second feature, e.g. nearly 3,000 scholars studying grammar, logic and philosophy, or selective admission

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj produced no lasting victor.
Reason (R): The three rival powers came from three different directions: the east, the west and the Deccan.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: there was no lasting victor because the three powers warred repeatedly through the 8th and 9th centuries with fluctuating outcomes; the directions they came from do not explain that.

questions.q: Vikramashila had six colleges and nearly 3,000 scholars. (a) If the scholars were spread equally, about how many would each college hold? (b) Why must your answer be called an estimate and not an exact count? (c) Each college had a scholar gatekeeper who tested students. Explain how this fits the chapter's description of admission.
questions.a: (a) 3,000 / 6 = 500 scholars per college, about. (b) The chapter says 'nearly' 3,000, which is an approximate figure, and the colleges need not have been of equal size. (c) Admission was highly selective: the dvarapandita of each college tested students before allowing them entry, so only those who passed could study there.
s: (a) About 500 per college (3,000 / 6)
(b) 'Nearly 3,000' is approximate and colleges need not be equal
(c) Gatekeepers tested students, so admission was highly selective

questions.q:
A Class 7 club in Varanasi designs a board game called 'Kannauj'. Three players start from three corners of the board: one from Bengal in the east, one from the region between Gujarat and Rajasthan in the west, and one from the Deccan. The game covers two centuries, the 8th and the 9th. The first draft of the rules says: 'The first player to capture Kannauj wins and keeps the city for ever.'
(a) Name the dynasty each of the three players represents.
(b) What does the word 'tripartite' mean, and why does it fit this game?
(c) Does the 'keeps the city for ever' rule match what happened? Explain from the chapter.
(d) Suggest a fairer ending rule and support it with one event from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) East: the Palas; west: the Gurjara-Pratiharas ('Gurjara' was the region between Gujarat and Rajasthan); Deccan: the Rashtrakutas. (b) Tripartite means involving three distinct parties; the game has three rival players. (c) No. The three powers repeatedly warred during the 8th and 9th centuries with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor. (d) For example: 'Kannauj may change hands; the game ends after the 9th century with no permanent winner.' Support: Bhoja of the Pratiharas held an empire reaching Kannauj, the Rashtrakutas briefly occupied Kannauj and later destroyed it, so control kept shifting.
s: (a) Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas matched to east, west and Deccan
(b) Tripartite = three distinct parties; three players
(c) No: repeated wars with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor
(d) A rule in which control can change, supported by an event such as the Rashtrakutas briefly occupying Kannauj

questions.q: Which Rashtrakuta king got the Kailashanatha temple carved out of a hillside at Ellora?
questions.a: Krishna I; the Kailashanatha temple at Ellora is the largest rock-cut temple in India.

questions.q: The chapter says that Dantidurga's successors 'campaigned successfully in north India, briefly occupying Kannauj'. What does this tell us?
o: A dynasty based in the Deccan also joined the contest for the Ganga plains
The Rashtrakutas moved their capital from Manyakheta to Kannauj for good
The Palas handed Kannauj over to the Rashtrakutas as a gift
The Rashtrakutas ended the Tripartite Struggle with a lasting victory
questions.a: A Deccan dynasty also joined the contest for the Ganga plains: the Rashtrakutas, ruling from Manyakheta in Karnataka, were one of the three parties in the struggle for Kannauj, and their hold on it was brief.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty was founded in the mid-8th century by Nagabhata I.
II. King Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratiharas was a devotee of Shiva.
III. Amoghavarsha I took the title 'Nripatunga', meaning 'peak of kings'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: Bhoja was a devotee of Vishnu, also called Adi Varaha.

questions.q: King Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratiharas was known by other names too. Name two of them and say what each refers to.
questions.a: 'Mihira', which is a name of the Sun; and 'Adi Varaha', after Varaha, the avatar of Vishnu in the form of a boar.
s: Mihira, a name of the Sun
Adi Varaha, from Varaha, Vishnu's boar avatar

questions.q: True or False: The early capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas was Bhillamala, which is modern Bhinmal in western Rajasthan. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter names Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal in western Rajasthan) as their early capital; it seems to have shifted later to Ujjayini.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Bhillamala/Bhinmal was the early capital, later apparently shifted to Ujjayini

questions.q: A road in central Bengaluru, home to several government buildings, is named 'Nrupatunga Road' after a 9th-century king. Give three reasons from the chapter why a city in Karnataka today might choose to honour this king.
questions.a: Amoghavarsha I (Nripatunga): (1) despite frequent wars he ensured peace and prosperity in his empire; (2) his reign of 64 years gave the empire stability; (3) he was a fine poet who composed in Sanskrit and Kannada, the language of Karnataka, and his inscriptions are found in Karnataka in old Kannada script. (He also patronised both Jainism and Hindu temples.)
s: Reason 1: peace and prosperity despite frequent wars
Reason 2: stability from a 64-year reign
Reason 3: poet in Sanskrit and Kannada, linking him to Karnataka (or patron of Jain and Hindu faiths)

questions.q: A Kannada literary society in Mysuru plans a talk titled 'The Rashtrakutas: Kings of Kannada Alone'. (a) Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter that the Rashtrakutas promoted Kannada. (b) Give two pieces of evidence that they promoted other languages too. (c) Decide whether the title is accurate. (d) Suggest a better title and justify it.
questions.a: (a) The Rashtrakutas encouraged learning and literature in Kannada; Amoghavarsha I composed works in Kannada, and his inscription in a Karnataka village temple is in old Kannada script. (b) They also encouraged Sanskrit and Prakrit, and Amoghavarsha I composed in Sanskrit as well. (c) Not accurate: the word 'alone' is wrong, since they promoted three languages. (d) For example, 'The Rashtrakutas: Patrons of Kannada, Sanskrit and Prakrit', because the evidence shows Kannada flourishing alongside the other two.
s: (a) Two pieces of evidence for Kannada
(b) Two pieces of evidence for Sanskrit and Prakrit
(c) Judges the title inaccurate because of 'alone'
(d) A better title justified from the evidence

questions.q: Who composed the Rajatarangini, the 'River of Kings', and in which century?
questions.a: Kalhana, a Kashmiri scholar and poet, composed it in Sanskrit in the 12th century.

questions.q: Adi Shankaracharya established four mathas. Which of these places was NOT one of them?
questions.a: Kanchipuram; the four mathas were at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Despite its mountainous geography, Kashmir remained well connected to developments elsewhere in India.
Reason (R): Scholars, monks and texts travelled between Kashmir and other parts of northern India, and Kashmiri artisans and manuscript painters were in demand across north India.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the movement of scholars, monks and texts, and the demand for Kashmiri artisans, is what kept the mountain kingdom linked to the cultural life of the subcontinent.

questions.q: Adi Shankaracharya was the 8th-century teacher of the advaita vedanta school. State two ideas he taught.
questions.a: (1) Brahman is the ultimate reality, or pure consciousness. (2) The world as we perceive it is maya, or illusion.
s: Brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness
The world as we perceive it is maya (illusion)

questions.q: Answer these about Kalhana's Rajatarangini. (a) In which language and in which century was it composed? (b) How many earlier works on the chronicles of kings did Kalhana say he examined? (c) Name two other kinds of records he consulted.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit, in the 12th century. (b) Eleven. (c) Any two: inscriptions relating to temple consecrations, royal grants, laudatory records, other written works.
s: (a) Sanskrit, 12th century
(b) Eleven earlier works
(c) Two of: temple consecration inscriptions, royal grants, laudatory records, other written works

questions.a: (a) Kalhana examined eleven earlier works and gave a connected account where the old narratives were fragmentary; Meera should read both booklets, compare them and join them into one account. (b) The plaques and registers are like the inscriptions on temple consecrations, royal grants and laudatory records that Kalhana consulted; such records helped him overcome many difficulties caused by errors. (c) Like a judge, a writer should relate past facts without favour or dislike; her grandfather's loving memories are valuable but must be checked against the registers and plaques. (d) Kalhana wanted to highlight rulers' ethical values and draw moral lessons from history; a school history need not preach lessons. (e) Her grandfather's memories (or a booklet written by an interested person), because affection can colour an account and memory can err; she should check it against written records first.
s: (a) Compare earlier accounts as Kalhana examined eleven works
(b) Plaques and registers like inscriptions and grants; they corrected errors
(c) Explains 'free from love or hatred' and applies it to the grandfather's memories
(d) Kalhana's aim of drawing moral lessons from rulers' conduct
(e) Picks the least trustworthy unchecked source with a reason

questions.q:
A museum in Leh is planning an exhibition on Kashmir between the 8th and 10th centuries. Its four exhibits are: a Buddhist manuscript carried from Kashmir to Tibet by a monk; an 8th-century stone sculpture of a standing Shiva from Kashmir; a page from the writings of Abhinavagupta; and a painted manuscript made by a Kashmiri painter but found far away in north India. The curator has to write the labels and choose a title.
(a) Name the school of thought that produced Abhinavagupta, and two fields his works covered.
(b) Besides Tibet, name two regions to and from which scholars, monks and texts travelled between them and Kashmir.
(c) What does the painted manuscript found in north India show about Kashmiri artisans of this time?
(d) The curator must choose between two titles: 'Kashmir: A Fortress Shut Away in the Mountains' and 'Kashmir: A Bridge of Learning and Art'. Choose one and justify your choice with two of the exhibits.
questions.a: (a) Kashmir Shaivism; his works covered any two of philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics, and had a vast influence across India. (b) Other parts of northern India and Central Asia. (c) Kashmiri artisans, sculptors and manuscript painters were in demand across north India and beyond. (d) 'Kashmir: A Bridge of Learning and Art'. Despite its mountainous geography Kashmir stayed well connected to the rest of India: the manuscript carried to Tibet shows it was a crucial bridge for Buddhist scholarship, and the painted manuscript found in north India and Abhinavagupta's writings, which influenced all of India, show its art and ideas reaching far beyond the valley.
s: (a) Kashmir Shaivism; two of philosophy, poetry, arts, aesthetics
(b) Other parts of northern India and Central Asia
(c) Kashmiri artisans, sculptors and painters were in demand across north India and beyond
(d) Chooses 'A Bridge of Learning and Art', justified with two exhibits

questions.q: Vatapi, the capital of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II, is known today as:
questions.a: Badami in Karnataka, famous for its complex of Hindu and Jain cave temples.

questions.q: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Badami. What happened next, according to the chapter?
o: He retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra as an unwritten boundary
He stayed on and moved the Pallava capital to Badami
He marched north and fought Harsha on the Narmada
He handed Badami to the Rashtrakutas for an alliance
questions.a: He retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra River as an unwritten boundary between the two powers.

questions.q:
Match each place in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Aihole  2. Badami  3. Vengi  4. Mamallapuram
Column II: P. Capital of the Eastern Chalukyas  Q. Seaport where ancient Chinese, Persian and Roman coins were found  R. Earlier Chalukya capital, home to over a hundred Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples  S. Chalukya capital famous for its Hindu and Jain cave temples
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Aihole was the earlier Chalukya capital with over a hundred temples; Badami (Vatapi) is famous for its cave temples; Vengi was the Eastern Chalukya capital; Mamallapuram was the seaport where Chinese, Persian and Roman coins were found.

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'monolithic' mean? (b) Give one example of monolithic work by the Pallavas.
questions.a: (a) Made of a single ('mono') stone or rock ('lithic'). (b) The monolithic temples carved at Mamallapuram.
s: (a) Made of a single stone or rock
(b) Monolithic temples at Mamallapuram

questions.q: True or False: Pulakeshin II, the Chalukya king who stopped Harsha's southward advance, was never defeated by any rival. Give the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Pulakeshin II eventually tasted defeat at the hands of the Pallavas of Kanchi; the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I defeated him and went on to capture Badami.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: he was defeated by the Pallavas of Kanchi under Narasimhavarman I, who captured Badami

questions.q: Kanchipuram under the Pallavas was both an economic and a cultural centre. (a) Name two goods traded there. (b) Name two lands the Pallavas traded with. (c) Name one poet who lived under the Pallavas.
questions.a: (a) Any two: spices, textiles (including silk), ivory, other luxury goods. (b) Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. (c) Dandin, who wrote elaborate Sanskrit poetry (or Mahendravarman I, who left a satirical Sanskrit play).
s: (a) Two goods such as spices, silk textiles, ivory
(b) Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
(c) Dandin (or Mahendravarman I)

questions.q:
A student claims: 'The Pallava victory over Pulakeshin II settled the Pallava-Chalukya rivalry for good and made the Pallavas masters of the Deccan.' Evaluate the claim.
(a) State what Narasimhavarman I achieved against the Chalukyas.
(b) State what he did after the victory, and what this means for the words 'masters of the Deccan'.
(c) State the span of the Pallava-Chalukya struggle as the chapter's timeline gives it, and what this shows about 'for good'.
(d) State how and when the Pallavas themselves lost power.
(e) Give your final verdict on the claim, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) He defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Badami, the Chalukya capital. (b) He retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra River as an unwritten boundary, so he did not rule the Deccan. (c) The timeline shows the struggle running from the 6th to the 8th century, so one victory in the 7th century did not end it. (d) They ruled much of northern Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra Pradesh until the late 9th century, when the Chola king Aditya I overthrew them. (e) The claim is wrong: the victory was real but neither final nor a conquest of the Deccan; the rivalry went on, and by the mid-8th century it was the Rashtrakutas, not the Pallavas, who replaced the Chalukyas in the Deccan.
s: (a) Defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Badami
(b) Retreated with the Tungabhadra as boundary, so not masters of the Deccan
(c) Struggle from the 6th to the 8th century, so not settled for good
(d) Overthrown by the Chola king Aditya I in the late 9th century
(e) Verdict: claim wrong, with reason

questions.q: Vijayalaya revived the Chola power in the 9th century. Which city did he make his new capital?
questions.a: Thanjavur (Tanjavur), from where he laid the foundation of a strong and prosperous kingdom.

questions.q: Researchers in Southeast Asia study coins of a south Indian dynasty whose capital was Madurai and whose power the Cholas swept aside in the 10th century. Which pairing of the dynasty and the port through which it traded with Southeast Asia is correct?
questions.a: Pandyas: Korkai. The dynasty with its capital at Madurai, swept aside by the Cholas in the 10th century, was the Pandyas, and their coins and inscriptions attest to maritime trade with Southeast Asia via ports such as Korkai.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Along the Kerala coast, the Cheras, also called Chera Perumals, kept their independence despite their neighbours' military power.
II. Aditya I, the son of Vijayalaya, expanded the Chola kingdom by defeating the Pallavas.
III. Chola dominance in south India lasted until the 13th century.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are correct.

questions.q: The Pandyas rose to power by the 6th century, with their capital at Madurai. (a) Which dynasty swept them aside, and in which century? (b) A heritage-walk guide calls the Pandyas 'warriors with no interest in trade or culture'. Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter against this.
questions.a: (a) The Cholas, in the 10th century. (b) Any two: their coins and inscriptions attest to maritime trade with Southeast Asia via ports such as Korkai; their capital Madurai was a vibrant cultural centre; they built many temples and created rock-cut temples; they patronised poets; a copper plate mentions their translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil.
s: (a) The Cholas, 10th century
(b) Two pieces of evidence of trade or culture (e.g. trade via Korkai, temples, patronage of poets)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the 10th century the Pandyas lost their hold over southern Tamil Nadu.
Reason (R): In the 10th century the Pandyas were swept aside by the Pallavas.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: in the 10th century it was the mighty Cholas who swept the Pandyas aside (the Pallavas had already been overthrown by the Chola king Aditya I in the late 9th century).

questions.q: A quiz book states: 'The Chola empire was built by war alone.' Is the claim right, partly right or wrong? Support your verdict with facts from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. War did matter: Aditya I expanded the kingdom by defeating the Pallavas, and the Cholas had a powerful navy. But war was not all: the empire was known for its elaborate and efficient administration; the fertile Kaveri delta and efficient irrigation gave a steady agricultural output that made the heartland prosperous; and they patronised temples, sculpture, architecture and Tamil and Sanskrit literature. So the claim captures one part of the story only.
s: Military evidence: Aditya I defeating the Pallavas, powerful navy
Non-military evidence: efficient administration, Kaveri delta and irrigation, patronage of arts
Verdict: partly right, with reason

questions.q:
A museum in Thanjavur sets up a gallery on the early Cholas. Its first panel reads: 'In the 9th century, Vijayalaya revived the Chola line and ruled from this very city. His son pushed north and defeated an old ruling family whose capital was Kanchi, bringing most of present-day Tamil Nadu and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh under Chola control. Chola dominance in the south would last until the 13th century.'
(a) Name Vijayalaya's son, who is mentioned in the panel.
(b) Name the ruling family with its capital at Kanchi that he defeated.
(c) The gallery's centrepiece is an early Chola bronze of Shiva as the 'Lord of dance'. Name this form and say what it symbolises.
(d) Using the panel's dates, about how many centuries did Chola power last, from Vijayalaya's revival to the end of its dominance?
questions.a: (a) Aditya I. (b) The Pallavas. (c) Nataraja; it symbolises the dance of creation and destruction of the universe. (d) From the 9th century to the 13th century, about four centuries.
s: (a) Aditya I
(b) The Pallavas
(c) Nataraja, the dance of creation and destruction of the universe
(d) About four centuries (9th to 13th)

questions.q: A king rules his core region directly. A distant region is run by a subordinate ruler who leads armies and manages local administration there for the king. What does the chapter call such a subordinate ruler?
questions.a: A samanta, the equivalent of a tributary or vassal, through whom kings such as the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas governed regions outside their core.

questions.q: How did the Kayasthas become a distinct jati, according to the chapter?
o: A professional group of scribes, open to different varnas, came to marry mainly within itself by about the 10th century
A tribe from the border regions was absorbed into the varna system and came to be counted as rulers and warriors
A group of foreign traders settled on the coast and stayed outside the varna-jati system as a separate community
A family of Shudra origin founded a dynasty and over time came to be regarded as Kshatriyas
questions.a: The Kayasthas, scribes or clerks, were first a professional group open to different varnas; in the 10th century they became a distinct jati, and over time they married mainly within their group.

questions.q:
Match each unit or body in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Bhukti (or rashtra)  2. Mandala  3. Village  4. Sabha
Column II: P. A district  Q. A province  R. The lowest administrative unit, overseen by headmen, accountants and local committees  S. A village assembly whose members' selection is detailed in Chola inscriptions at Uttaramerur
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Bhukti or rashtra = province; mandala = district; village = the lowest, largely self-governed unit; sabha = the village assembly described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions.

questions.q: True or False: Many of the tanks that the Pallavas built in Tamil Nadu are still in use today. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the Pallavas built numerous tanks in Tamil Nadu, many of which are still functional today; they were part of the irrigation works of this period that helped expand agriculture.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the Pallavas built numerous tanks, many still functional today, as part of the period's irrigation works

questions.q: A textbook photograph shows a 7th-century hero stone from Eduthanur, a village in Tamil Nadu, carved with a local chief and his dog. (a) What does the inscription on the stone praise the chief and the dog for, and what happened to them? (b) What danger to village life at that time does this point to? (c) The inscription gives the names of both the chief and the dog. What does this suggest about how the people saw their deed?
questions.a: (a) It praises the chief who, along with his loyal dog, fought cattle thieves; both of them lost their lives. (b) Cattle thieves raided villages, so a village's cattle could be stolen and local chiefs had to defend them, even at the cost of their lives. (c) Even the dog's loyalty and sacrifice were honoured and remembered, showing that the community valued courage and loyalty enough to record them in stone.
s: (a) Praised for fighting cattle thieves; both the chief and the dog lost their lives
(b) Cattle theft or raids were a danger that local chiefs defended against
(c) The dog's loyalty and sacrifice were honoured; bravery and loyalty were valued

questions.q:
A website claims: 'Between the 6th and 10th centuries India was cut off from the rest of the world; its people only farmed and traded inside their own regions.' Evaluate the claim.
(a) State which lands India's west coast traded with from the 8th century.
(b) State which lands India's east coast connected with.
(c) Give one piece of evidence that foreign traders lived and worked in India.
(d) State the role of ship-owning merchants and of merchant guilds in this trade.
(e) Give your verdict: which part of the claim has some truth, and why is the claim wrong overall?
questions.a: (a) Ports in present-day Iran, Iraq and Africa's east coast. (b) Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and all the way to Chinese ports. (c) A set of copper-plate inscriptions refers to Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders from West Asia. (d) Small traders handled local trade while ship-owning merchants conducted long-distance commerce; merchant guilds of traders, artisans and moneylenders played a significant role, one in south India becoming the largest inter-regional merchant association. (e) It is true that society remained largely rural and agrarian, but the claim is wrong overall: brisk shipping on both coasts connected local economies with distant markets, and India was a hub of international trade.
s: (a) West coast: Iran, Iraq, east coast of Africa
(b) East coast: Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, China
(c) Copper plates naming Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders from West Asia
(d) Ship-owning merchants for long-distance trade; guilds of traders, artisans and moneylenders
(e) Verdict: largely rural and agrarian, but connected to distant markets, so the claim is wrong overall

questions.q: In which work did Brahmagupta introduce the rules of arithmetic with zero, negative numbers and fractions?
questions.a: Brahmasphutasiddhanta, Brahmagupta's major work.

questions.q: A Tamil poem of devotion to Vishnu from this period was composed by a woman poet-saint. Who could she be, and to which group of devotees did she belong?
o: Karaikal Ammaiyar, one of the Alvars
Karaikal Ammaiyar, one of the Nayanars
questions.a: Andal, one of the Alvars: the 12 Alvars were devotees of Vishnu and one of them, Andal, was a woman. Karaikal Ammaiyar was a woman saint among the Nayanars, who were devotees of Shiva.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Jainism remained popular in western India and Karnataka during this period.
Reason (R): The monolithic statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola was made in the 10th century.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the Bahubali statue is one monument of the period, while Jainism stayed popular because it was supported by rulers and wealthy merchant communities.

questions.q: How did the Puranas shape religious life in this period? State two ways.
questions.a: (1) With their mythology and sacred geography, they helped integrate local deities and regional myths into the broader pan-Indian cults, especially of Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna and various devis. (2) These traditions emphasised bhakti (personal devotion) over Vedic sacrifices and centred on temples, mathas and pilgrimage sites.
s: Integrated local deities and regional myths into pan-Indian cults
Emphasised bhakti over Vedic sacrifices, centred on temples, mathas and pilgrimage sites

questions.q: Answer these about Brahmagupta. (a) Where and in which year was he born? (b) Name two kinds of numbers whose arithmetic rules he introduced. (c) Into which languages were his works later translated?
questions.a: (a) In Bhillamala, in 598 CE. (b) Any two: zero, negative numbers, fractions. (c) Persian, and later Latin.
s: (a) Bhillamala, 598 CE
(b) Two of zero, negative numbers, fractions
(c) Persian and later Latin

questions.q: Your class is making a 'Who did what?' chart of four scholars of this period for the maths corner. For each, write one contribution that the chapter credits to them: (a) Bhaskara I; (b) Virahanka; (c) Mahavira, the Jain mathematician; (d) Brahmagupta, other than his rules of arithmetic.
questions.a: (a) Bhaskara I did pioneering work in trigonometry and wrote a lengthy commentary on the Aryabhatiya. (b) Virahanka was the first to establish the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence. (c) Mahavira, who lived at the court of Amoghavarsha Nripatunga, wrote the first work of mathematics independent of astronomy. (d) Brahmagupta pioneered new techniques for solving certain equations, making him one of the founders of modern algebra.
s: (a) Bhaskara I: trigonometry, commentary on the Aryabhatiya
(b) Virahanka: the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence
(c) Mahavira: first mathematics work independent of astronomy
(d) Brahmagupta: techniques for solving equations, a founder of algebra

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' is borrowed from an Arabic word. Which word, and what does it mean?
questions.a: mawsim, the Arabic word for 'season'; ships sailed between India and Arabia with the monsoon winds.

questions.q: On a school trip to Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh (ancient Dashapura), students see twin victory pillars. What do the inscriptions on these pillars commemorate?
o: The Aulikara king Yashodharma's victory over a Huna leader
Nagabhata I's victory over a large Arab army
Lalitaditya Muktapida's victory over an Arab chief
Muhammad bin Qasim's victory over King Dahar
questions.a: The Aulikara king Yashodharma's victory over a Huna leader; the Aulikara kings of Dashapura defeated the Hunas, ending Huna power in India.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. The Arab naval raids of 637 on Thana, Bharuch and Debal gave the Arabs lasting control of these ports.
II. Muhammad bin Qasim led an army sent by the governor of Iraq, who was his uncle and father-in-law.
III. Debal fell to bin Qasim only after he had defeated King Dahar at Aror.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: II only. Statement I is wrong because the 637 raids secured no lasting territorial control. Statement III is wrong because Debal fell first; bin Qasim then moved east to Aror, Dahar's capital.

questions.q: The Chachnama records how two queens responded after King Dahar was killed. (a) What did his widowed queen do? (b) Another queen ordered her treasure to be distributed among the brave soldiers. Suggest why she did this.
questions.a: (a) She put up a brave resistance and, when the situation became hopeless, immolated herself along with other ladies. (b) To reward the soldiers and inspire them to keep standing against the invaders.
s: (a) Resisted bravely, then immolated herself with other ladies when all was hopeless
(b) To reward and inspire the soldiers to keep resisting the invaders

questions.q:
A student writes: 'Contact between India and Arabia began with the Arab invasions and was only about war.' Evaluate the statement.
(a) State how India and Arabia were connected before the rise of Islam.
(b) Show how the word 'monsoon' is evidence of this contact.
(c) Give one more piece of word evidence from the chapter's table.
(d) State what happened to Indian scientific texts in the 9th century.
(e) Explain the journey of India's numerals and give your verdict on the statement.
questions.a: (a) Long before the rise of Islam, India and Arabia were well connected through trade, with ships sailing back and forth with the monsoon winds, carrying spices, textiles, ideas, languages and stories. (b) 'Monsoon' is borrowed from the Arabic mawsim, 'season', a word picked up through this sea trade. (c) For example, Sanskrit karpura and English camphor, Sanskrit pippali and Arabic filfil, or Sanskrit tambula and Arabic tanbul sound alike. (d) Sanskrit texts of mathematics, astronomy and medicine were translated into Arabic, notably in Baghdad. (e) The Arabs adopted India's decimal system with zero and passed it to Europe, where the numerals were called 'Arabic numerals'; Arab mathematicians acknowledged the Indian origin and dictionaries now say 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'. Verdict: the statement is wrong; contact began long before the invasions and was largely about trade, words and knowledge.
s: (a) Trade before Islam, ships sailing with the monsoon winds
(b) 'Monsoon' from Arabic mawsim, 'season'
(c) Another similar-sounding word pair from the table
(d) 9th-century translation of Sanskrit maths, astronomy and medicine texts into Arabic
(e) Numerals passed through the Arabs to Europe; verdict that the statement is wrong

questions.q: Tanya says: 'The Hunas were never defeated in India; they simply settled down and became part of Indian society.' Is she right, partly right or wrong? Give evidence from the chapter for your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that by the 7th century the Hunas had assimilated: many served as soldiers or in local administration (one sat on a temple's administration council), and they used Sanskrit and Prakrit, Gupta-style titles, coin designs and religious symbols. But she is wrong that they were never defeated: in the early 6th century two Huna leaders who pushed deep into the Ganga plains were defeated by the Aulikara kings of Dashapura (Mandsaur), whose victory pillars still stand, and these defeats ended Huna power in India.
s: Correct part: assimilation by the 7th century, with evidence
Wrong part: defeated by the Aulikara kings of Dashapura, ending Huna power
Verdict: partly right, with reason
